question: The sidereal period of Mars is 687 days, while the sidereal period of Earth is 365.26 days. The most recent opposition of Mars occurred on July 27, 2018. Predict all dates in the year 2020 when Mars will be in quadrature. You may use the fact that the orbital radius of Mars is 1.52 AU and that Earth and Mars have circular orbits. Why might your answer be inaccurate?
answer: The synodic period is computed as 1/P_syn = 1/P_Earth − 1/P_Mars. Using the values given, P_syn = 779.9 days. Thus oppositions happen every 779.9 days, so the next one will be around 9/15/2020. Quadrature occurs when Mars is approximately arccos(1/1.52)=48.9 degrees behind or in front of its position at opposition, or 779.9×(48.9/360)=106 days before or after opposition. The only such date in 2020 is around 6/2/2020; accept answers within two days. Inaccuracies could be due to nonzero eccentricities of Earth and Mars and the nonzero relative inclination between the two planets' orbits. The actual date is nearer 6/7/2020.

question: The star Betelgeuse has recently made news for its abnormal dimming. Although the dimming has now been attributed to dust, we consider in this problem that it was due to radial pulsations. Suppose that Betelgeuse's mass is 11 solar masses and its radius is 887 solar radii. Furthermore, Betelgeuse is currently rotating such that the tangential velocity of a point on its equator is 5000 m/s (assume Betelgeuse is perfectly spherical). The dimming has increased Betelgeuse's apparent magnitude by 1.05. You may neglect the contribution of pulsation to the surface velocity. Assuming contraction and expansion are isothermal, find the new radius of the star in solar radii needed to account for the dimming.
answer: An increase in apparent magnitude of 1.05 corresponds to a decrease in brightness by a factor of 100^(1.05/5)=0.38. This is the ratio of final to initial luminosity. Applying the Stefan-Boltzmann law, L_f/L_i = R_f^2/R_i^2, so the final radius is 547 solar radii.

question: The star Betelgeuse has recently made news for its abnormal dimming. Although the dimming has now been attributed to dust, we consider in this problem that it was due to radial pulsations. Suppose that Betelgeuse's mass is 11 solar masses and its radius is 887 solar radii. Furthermore, Betelgeuse is currently rotating such that the tangential velocity of a point on its equator is 5000 m/s (assume Betelgeuse is perfectly spherical). The dimming has increased Betelgeuse's apparent magnitude by 1.05. You may neglect the contribution of pulsation to the surface velocity. Assuming no mass loss, find the new angular rotation velocity of the star.
answer: Apply conservation of angular momentum. The initial angular velocity is ω_i = v_T/R_i = 8.10×10^-9 rad/s. The initial moment of inertia is I_i = (2/5)MR_i^2 = 3.34×10^54 kg m^2 and the final moment of inertia is I_f = (2/5)MR_f^2 = 1.27×10^54 kg m^2. From I_i ω_i = I_f ω_f, ω_f = 2.13×10^-8 rad/s.

question: The Lyman-break galaxy selection technique makes use of the fact that any light from galaxies with wavelength shorter than the Lyman limit (the shortest wavelength in the Lyman series) is essentially totally absorbed by neutral gas surrounding the galaxies. The ionization energy of hydrogen is 13.6 eV. Suppose that we are observing galaxies in the V band, whose effective midpoint is 551 nm and bandwidth is 99 nm. At what range of redshifts would we begin to see galaxies disappear (break) from images in the V band?
answer: The Lyman limit is obtained from E = hc/λ_L = 13.6 eV, so λ_L = 91.2 nm. For the V band, λ_max = 600.5 nm and λ_min = 501.5 nm. Applying z = Δλ/λ_L, the desired range of redshifts is z = 4.50–5.58.

question: The Lyman-break galaxy selection technique makes use of the fact that any light from galaxies with wavelength shorter than the Lyman limit (the shortest wavelength in the Lyman series) is essentially totally absorbed by neutral gas surrounding the galaxies. The ionization energy of hydrogen is 13.6 eV. Suppose that we are observing galaxies in the V band, whose effective midpoint is 551 nm and bandwidth is 99 nm. What range of recessional velocities in km/s and distances in Mpc does this correspond to? Assume only Hubble expansion contributes to the radial velocity and redshift.
answer: Using relativistic Doppler shift, v_rel = ((1+z)^2 − 1)/((1+z)^2 + 1)c. For z = 4.50–5.58, the range of recessional velocities is v_rel = 281,000–286,000 km/s. Applying Hubble's law, the range of distances is 4010–4090 Mpc.

question: TRAPPIST-1d is a temperate exoplanet that orbits the ultra-cool M dwarf star TRAPPIST-1 with a semi-major axis of 0.022 AU. TRAPPIST-1 has a mass of 0.089 solar masses and an effective temperature of 2511 K. Through transit timing variations induced by other planets in the TRAPPIST-1 system, TRAPPIST-1d is estimated to have a mass of 0.297 Earth masses. Assuming that TRAPPIST-1d has a circular orbit (which is a good approximation because the measured eccentricity is only 0.008), what is the radial velocity semi-amplitude of TRAPPIST-1 due to the orbital motion of TRAPPIST-1d, in m/s?
answer: M_p/M_star = V_star/V_p, so V_star = M_p V_p/M_star. V_p = 2πa/T. From Kepler's third law, T = ([a(AU)]^3/[M_star(M_sun)])^(1/2) × 365.25 days/year = (0.022^3/0.089)^(1/2) × 365.25 = 4.00 days. Then V_p = 2π(0.022 AU × 1.496×10^11 m)/(4.00 days × 86400 s/day) = 59.8 km/s. Therefore V_star = (0.297×5.97×10^24 kg×59.8×10^3 m/s)/(0.089×1.99×10^30 kg)=0.597 m/s. The radial velocity semi-amplitude is 0.597 m/s.

question: HD 209458b is a hot Jupiter exoplanet with a mass of 0.69 Jupiter masses. However, HD 209458b has an anomalous radius of 1.38 Jupiter radii that is inflated relative to Jupiter. Jupiter has an interior that is comprised of metallic hydrogen at pressures greater than 1 Mbar. Estimate the pressure, in Mbar, at the center of HD 209458b, and determine whether or not the interior of HD 209458b will also be comprised of metallic hydrogen.
answer: Estimate P_c ~ ρgR ~ 3GM^2/(4πR^4). The actual solution is P_c = 3GM^2/(8πR^4). Plugging in, P_c = 3×6.67×10^-11×(0.69×1.898×10^27 kg)^2/(8π(1.38×69.91×10^6 m)^4) = 1.57 Mbar. The estimate gives twice the value, 3.15 Mbar, because it ignores the integral; this is acceptable because no calculus is required. Accept answers between 1 and 5 Mbar. Yes, the interior of HD 209458b will be composed of metallic hydrogen.

question: An astronomer used his f/5 telescope with a diameter of 130 mm to observe a binary system. He is using an eyepiece with a field of view of 45° and a focal length of 25 mm. In this system, star A has a mass of 18.9 solar masses and apparent magnitude in the V filter of 9.14. Star B has a mass of 16.2 solar masses and apparent magnitude in the V filter of 9.60. The period of the system is 108 days, and the distance between the binary stars and the Solar System is 2.29 kpc. The binary system has an edge-on orbit relative to the Solar System. The limiting magnitude for the human eye is 6.0, and the diameter of the pupil is 7.0 mm. Also consider that visible light has a wavelength of 550 nm. What is the field of view of the telescope?
answer: Divide the field of view of the eyepiece by the magnification of the telescope: FOV_telescope = FOV_eyepiece/m = FOV_eyepiece/(f_telescope/f_eyepiece) = 45°/((130×5)/25) = 1.7°.

question: An astronomer used his f/5 telescope with a diameter of 130 mm to observe a binary system. He is using an eyepiece with a field of view of 45° and a focal length of 25 mm. In this system, star A has a mass of 18.9 solar masses and apparent magnitude in the V filter of 9.14. Star B has a mass of 16.2 solar masses and apparent magnitude in the V filter of 9.60. The period of the system is 108 days, and the distance between the binary stars and the Solar System is 2.29 kpc. The binary system has an edge-on orbit relative to the Solar System. The limiting magnitude for the human eye is 6.0, and the diameter of the pupil is 7.0 mm. Also consider that visible light has a wavelength of 550 nm. What is the limiting magnitude of the telescope?
answer: Use m_eye − m_telescope = 2.5 log(D_eye^2/D_telescope^2). Then 6.0 − m_telescope = 2.5 log(7^2/130^2), so m_telescope = 12.3. Since both stars are brighter than the limiting magnitude, both can be detected by the telescope.

answer: The angular resolution is θ = 1.22λ/D_telescope = 1.22×550×10^-9/(130×10^-3) = 5.16×10^-6 rad.

question: An astronomer used his f/5 telescope with a diameter of 130 mm to observe a binary system. He is using an eyepiece with a field of view of 45° and a focal length of 25 mm. In this system, star A has a mass of 18.9 solar masses and apparent magnitude in the V filter of 9.14. Star B has a mass of 16.2 solar masses and apparent magnitude in the V filter of 9.60. The period of the system is 108 days, and the distance between the binary stars and the Solar System is 2.29 kpc. The binary system has an edge-on orbit relative to the Solar System. The limiting magnitude for the human eye is 6.0, and the diameter of the pupil is 7.0 mm. Also consider that visible light has a wavelength of 550 nm. What is the angular separation between the stars?
answer: Using Kepler's third law, T^2/a^3 = 1/M, so (108/365.25 years)^2/a^3 = 1/(18.9+16.2), giving a = 1.45 AU. Dividing by the distance gives angular separation α = a/d = 1.45 AU/(2.29×10^3×206265 AU)=3.08×10^-9 rad.

question: An astronomer used his f/5 telescope with a diameter of 130 mm to observe a binary system. He is using an eyepiece with a field of view of 45° and a focal length of 25 mm. In this system, star A has a mass of 18.9 solar masses and apparent magnitude in the V filter of 9.14. Star B has a mass of 16.2 solar masses and apparent magnitude in the V filter of 9.60. The period of the system is 108 days, and the distance between the binary stars and the Solar System is 2.29 kpc. The binary system has an edge-on orbit relative to the Solar System. The limiting magnitude for the human eye is 6.0, and the diameter of the pupil is 7.0 mm. Also consider that visible light has a wavelength of 550 nm. Is the astronomer able to observe both stars as distinct points in the telescope? Answer as YES or NO.
answer: Since the angular separation between the stars is smaller than the angular resolution, the astronomer will observe both stars as a single point. Therefore, the correct answer is NO.

question: The rotation curve of a particular spiral galaxy is modeled by an exponential function V(r)=V_0(1−e^(−r/R)), where V_0=250 km/s, R=7.5 kpc, and r is measured radially from the center of the galaxy. Throughout parts (a)-(d), you may assume the galaxy is disk-shaped. Further, assume that the distribution of mass in the galaxy depends only on the radial coordinate r and is radially symmetric. Find the period of rotation in years of a particle 10 kpc from the center of the galaxy. Also find the mass enclosed within the circular orbit in solar masses, i.e. the mass within r=10 kpc from the center of the galaxy.
answer: The period is T = 2πr/V, so T = 334 million years. Equating centripetal force with gravitational force gives M = V^2 r/G, so M = 7.88×10^10 solar masses.

question: The rotation curve of a particular spiral galaxy is modeled by an exponential function V(r)=V_0(1−e^(−r/R)), where V_0=250 km/s, R=7.5 kpc, and r is measured radially from the center of the galaxy. Throughout parts (a)-(d), you may assume the galaxy is disk-shaped. Further, assume that the distribution of mass in the galaxy depends only on the radial coordinate r and is radially symmetric. Find the angular velocity of the galaxy very close to the center (r << R). Hint: e^x ≈ 1+x for |x| << 1.
answer: ω = V/r. Very close to the center, e^(−r/R) ≈ 1 − r/R, so ω ≈ V_0/R = 1.08×10^-15 rad/s.

question: The rotation curve of a particular spiral galaxy is modeled by an exponential function V(r)=V_0(1−e^(−r/R)), where V_0=250 km/s, R=7.5 kpc, and r is measured radially from the center of the galaxy. Throughout parts (a)-(d), you may assume the galaxy is disk-shaped. Further, assume that the distribution of mass in the galaxy depends only on the radial coordinate r and is radially symmetric. Determine how the gravitational mass per unit area must vary with distance from the center of the galaxy in order to yield the given rotation curve. Find the expressions only for regions very far from the galactic center.
answer: Recall M = V^2 r/G. Consider an annulus at radius r with small thickness δr. Let σ be mass per unit area, so σ 2πr δr = δM. Far from the center, V is essentially constant, so δM ≈ V^2 δr/G. Thus σ = V_0^2/(2πrG) very far from the center (r >> R).

question: The rotation curve of a particular spiral galaxy is modeled by an exponential function V(r)=V_0(1−e^(−r/R)), where V_0=250 km/s, R=7.5 kpc, and r is measured radially from the center of the galaxy. Throughout parts (a)-(d), you may assume the galaxy is disk-shaped. Further, assume that the distribution of mass in the galaxy depends only on the radial coordinate r and is radially symmetric. An astronomer measures the absolute bolometric magnitude of the galaxy to be −21.2. The bolometric magnitude of the sun is 4.75. Assume that the luminous mass per unit area follows σ_L=k/r for k=2.55×10^8 M_sun/kpc and all luminous mass is in Sun-like stars. Approximate the percentage of the galaxy mass that is dark matter out to the maximum radius that is still visibly defined.
answer: M_bol = 4.75 − 2.5 log(L/L_sun), so L/L_sun = 2.40×10^10. The luminous mass enclosed in an annulus is 2πrδr σ_L = 2πkδr, so 2πk r_max = 2.40×10^10. This gives r_max = 14.97 kpc. The gravitational mass enclosed at this radius is M = V^2 r/G = 1.63×10^11 solar masses. The dark matter fraction is approximately 1 − (2.40×10^10)/(1.63×10^11) = 85%.

question: An astro-photographer has taken the photo of the moon close to a new moon day shown below right before sunset on December 21 (Winter Solstice) in a wide open area. Find the latitude of the photographer. Ignore the orbital inclination of the Moon and the ellipticity of the Earth orbit. Hint: the green equiangular lines are added to help measure any relevant angle.
answer: Measure the angle between the horizon and ecliptic as about 40°. Let S be the celestial south pole, Z the zenith, and K′ the South ecliptic pole. Using the spherical geometry relationships and the spherical law of cosines, sin φ = cos 23.5° cos 40°, so φ = 44.6°. Since the photographer is in the Southern hemisphere, φ = 44.6° S.

question: An astro-photographer has taken the photo of the moon close to a new moon day shown below right before sunset on December 21 (Winter Solstice) in a wide open area. Calculate the sidereal time when the photo was taken.
answer: Sidereal time = H_sun + RA_sun. From the spherical law of cosines, cos H_sun = −tan 23.5° tan 44.6°, so H_sun = 7 h 42 m. At the Winter Solstice, RA_sun = 18 h, so ST = 7 h 42 m + 18 h = 1 h 42 m.

question: In general relativity, the orbit of satellites around a massive object, like a black hole, are known as geodesics and do not obey all of Kepler's laws for orbits. However, for objects moving at non-relativistic speeds, we can analyze the orbit using classical mechanics with a corrective term added to Newton's Law of gravity. The potential energy is V_s(r)=−GMm/r − GML^2/(c^2 m r^3), and the gravitational force magnitude is F_s(r)=GMm/r^2 + 3GML^2/(c^2 m r^4). Here M and m are the masses of the black hole and object, c is the speed of light, L is the angular momentum of the object, and r is the distance from the black hole. Assume conservation of energy and angular momentum hold. Argue which of Kepler's laws are still true.
answer: Only Kepler's law of areas still holds, because the force is radial.

question: In general relativity, the orbit of satellites around a massive object, like a black hole, are known as geodesics and do not obey all of Kepler's laws for orbits. However, for objects moving at non-relativistic speeds, we can analyze the orbit using classical mechanics with a corrective term added to Newton's Law of gravity. The potential energy is V_s(r)=−GMm/r − GML^2/(c^2 m r^3), and the gravitational force magnitude is F_s(r)=GMm/r^2 + 3GML^2/(c^2 m r^4). Here M and m are the masses of the black hole and object, c is the speed of light, L is the angular momentum of the object, and r is the distance from the black hole. Assume conservation of energy and angular momentum hold. Calculate the radius of a stable circular orbit with angular momentum L. You will get two solutions; the stable orbit generates the classical result under the proper limits.
answer: Using centripetal force, L^2/(m r^3)=GMm/r^2 + 3GML^2/(c^2 m r^4). Algebra gives r^2 − (L^2/(GMm^2))r + 3L^2/(m^2c^2)=0. Thus r = (L^2/(2GMm^2))(1 ± sqrt(1 − 12G^2M^2m^2/(L^2c^2))). Taking c→∞, the plus solution gives the classical result. The stable orbit is the plus solution and the unstable orbit is the minus solution.

question: In general relativity, the orbit of satellites around a massive object, like a black hole, are known as geodesics and do not obey all of Kepler's laws for orbits. The potential energy is V_s(r)=−GMm/r − GML^2/(c^2 m r^3), and the gravitational force magnitude is F_s(r)=GMm/r^2 + 3GML^2/(c^2 m r^4). Here M and m are the masses of the black hole and object, c is the speed of light, L is the angular momentum of the object, and r is the distance from the black hole. Assume conservation of energy and angular momentum hold. What is the radius R_ISCO of the innermost stable circular orbit for a black hole of mass M? What is the numerical value of R_ISCO for Sagittarius A*, which has mass 3.6×10^6 solar masses?
answer: The ISCO occurs at the smallest allowed L, where L^2 = 12G^2M^2m^2/c^2. This gives R_ISCO = 6GM/c^2. For Sagittarius A*, R_ISCO = 3.20×10^10 m ≈ 0.21 AU.

question: In general relativity, the orbit of satellites around a massive object, like a black hole, are known as geodesics and do not obey all of Kepler's laws for orbits. Find the magnitude of velocity of S99 at both periapsis and apoapsis.

The following table gives the numerical values for some physical properties of four stars. The quantities affected by interstellar extinction are marked with a star. question: M15 is a globular cluster in the constellation Pegasus. The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (apparent visual magnitude versus color index) of the cluster is shown in Figure 1. Considering that the mass-luminosity relation for main sequence stars is L/M^3 = constant, answer the following questions. Ignore interstellar reddening and dust extinction effects. Given that all the stars are formed at the same time, estimate the age of the globular cluster. The color index of the sun ((B−V)_sun) is 0.65 and its lifetime on the main sequence is 10 billion years.
answer: From the H-R diagram, a solar-like star with (B−V)_sun=0.65 has apparent visual magnitude V_sun=21.4. A star at the main-sequence turnoff has V_t=19.3. Thus V_sun−V_t = 2.5 log(L_t/L_sun), giving L_t/L_sun ~ 7. Main-sequence lifetime ∝ M/L ∝ L^(1/3)/L ∝ L^(−2/3), so the age is 10(L_t/L_sun)^(−2/3) billion years = 2.7 billion years. M15 is very metal-poor, so its actual age should be larger; the discrepancy can be explained by large uncertainty in B−V measurements.
caption: Figure 1: HR diagram for M15.

question: M15 is a globular cluster in the constellation Pegasus. The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (apparent visual magnitude versus color index) of the cluster is shown in Figure 1. Considering that the mass-luminosity relation for main sequence stars is L/M^3 = constant, answer the following questions. Ignore interstellar reddening and dust extinction effects. Estimate the distance of this globular cluster from Earth in parsec. The absolute visual magnitude of the Sun is 4.83.
answer: The distance modulus is V_sun − M_V(sun) = 21.4 − 4.83 = 16.57. Since distance modulus = 5 log(d(pc)/10), d ~ 20 kpc. The actual distance is ~10 kpc; the overestimate comes from ignoring dust extinction.
caption: Figure 1: HR diagram for M15.

question: M15 is a globular cluster in the constellation Pegasus. The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (apparent visual magnitude versus color index) of the cluster is shown in Figure 1. Considering that the mass-luminosity relation for main sequence stars is L/M^3 = constant, answer the following questions. Ignore interstellar reddening and dust extinction effects. Given that stars spend about 10% of their main-sequence lifetime in the post-main-sequence phase, find the mass of the most massive star in the post-main-sequence stage.
answer: The most massive star in the post-main-sequence phase spent 2.7/110% = 2.45 billion years on the main sequence. Main-sequence lifetime ∝ M/L ∝ M/M^3 ∝ M^−2, so M_max(post-main sequence) = (2.45/10)^−0.5 M_sun = 2.02 M_sun.
caption: Figure 1: HR diagram for M15.

question: M15 is a globular cluster in the constellation Pegasus. The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (apparent visual magnitude versus color index) of the cluster is shown in Figure 1. Considering that the mass-luminosity relation for main sequence stars is L/M^3 = constant, answer the following questions. Ignore interstellar reddening and dust extinction effects. The number of stars in the mass range (M1, M2) is N(M1 ≤ M ≤ M2)=A(M1^−1.35 − M2^−1.35), where A is a constant and M1 and M2 are in solar masses. Assuming that the number of stars in the post-main-sequence phase is 515, calculate A.
answer: The mass at the turnoff is (L_t/L_sun)^(1/3) = 7^(1/3) = 1.91 M_sun. Thus A = 515/(1.91^−1.35 − 2.02^−1.35) ~ 16945. This can change depending on normalization of masses; here M1 and M2 are in solar masses.
caption: Figure 1: HR diagram for M15.

question: M15 is a globular cluster in the constellation Pegasus. The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (apparent visual magnitude versus color index) of the cluster is shown in Figure 1. Considering that the mass-luminosity relation for main sequence stars is L/M^3 = constant, answer the following questions. Ignore interstellar reddening and dust extinction effects. M15 is densely packed such that in a visual band (λ ~ 5500 Å) image taken by a 10 cm telescope, the central stars cannot be resolved. Estimate the minimum number of stars in this cluster. The angular diameter of M15 is 12.3 arcmin. Assume constant number density within the cluster.
answer: Consider a cylinder with height 2R and diameter equal to the telescope resolution at the cluster center. It should contain at least two stars for unresolved central stars. Telescope resolution: θ = 1.22λ/D = 1.22(550 nm)/(0.1 m)=1.38 arcsec. Then 2/(2R × πD^2/4) = N_min/((4/3)πR^3), so N_min = (16/3)(R/D)^2 = (16/3)((12.3/2 arcmin)/(1.38 arcsec))^2 ~ 3.8×10^5.
caption: Figure 1: HR diagram for M15.

question: Figure 2 shows two magnetograms of the Sun taken with the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) at the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) toward the end of January 2020. The picture on the left was taken three days after the image on the right. Select the pair of images numbered I to V in which the lines are drawn at the Sun's Equator and the Xs correspond to the position of each sunspot 4 days before the pictures were taken.
answer: The correct answer is III.

question: Figure 2 shows two magnetograms of the Sun taken with the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) at the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) toward the end of January 2020. The picture on the left was taken three days after the image on the right. Estimate the absolute value of the latitude of both sunspots in Figure 2.
answer: The acceptable range is 26° to 29° for full credit, and 25° or 30° for half credit. It is useful to know that sunspots always come in pairs and have the same absolute value of latitude, one positive and one negative.
caption: Figure 2: Solar magnetograms taken at the end of January 2020.

question: Figure 2 shows two magnetograms of the Sun taken with the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) at the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) toward the end of January 2020. The picture on the left was taken three days after the image on the right. Figure 3 is a magnetogram of the Sun in normal activity. It is possible to notice that the sunspots have different orientations in different hemispheres. In one hemisphere, each spot has the white part on the left and the black part on the right, and vice versa. However, this is not the case for the images in Figure 2. Suggest an explanation for the anomaly.
answer: Every 11 years, the period of the Schwabe Cycle, the Solar magnetosphere flips its orientation. Therefore, the orientation of sunspots in each hemisphere is reversed. The pictures in part (a) were likely taken while the Sun was going through this transition, explaining the anomaly.
caption: Figure 3: Sun in normal activity.

question: Figure 2 shows two magnetograms of the Sun taken with the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) at the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) toward the end of January 2020. The picture on the left was taken three days after the image on the right. Assume for simplicity that a specific sunspot has a shape similar to a spherical triangle. The sides are 0.176°, 0.0981°, and 0.201°. Calculate the three internal angles in degrees.
answer: Let A, B, and C be the internal angles. Using the spherical law of cosines: cos(0.176°)=cos(0.0981°)cos(0.201°)+sin(0.0981°)sin(0.201°)cos(A), so A=61.11699°. Using the spherical law of sines, sin(61.11699°)/sin(0.176°)=sin(B)/sin(0.201°), giving B=89.67051°. Similarly, sin(61.11699°)/sin(0.176°)=sin(C)/sin(0.0981°), giving C=29.21265°.
caption: Figure 2: Solar magnetograms taken at the end of January 2020.

question: Figure 2 shows two magnetograms of the Sun taken with the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) at the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) toward the end of January 2020. The picture on the left was taken three days after the image on the right. Assume this sunspot is centered at 7.89° South and 51.74° East of the center of the Solar disk for an observer on Earth. What is the ratio between the area of the Solar disk and the observed area of the sunspot? The required ratio is for observed areas. The area of a spherical triangle is πR^2E/180°, where spherical excess E in degrees equals the sum of internal angles minus 180°.
answer: First compute spherical excess: E=61.1°+89.7°+29.2°−180°=1.51×10^-4 degrees. Then A=πR_sun^2×1.51×10^-4/180=8.41×10^-7 πR_sun^2. Correct for inclination of the tangential plane: cos(i)=cos(7.89°)cos(51.74°), so i=52.2°. Then A_c=8.41×10^-7 πR_sun^2 cos(52.2°)=5.16×10^-7 πR_sun^2. Since the Solar disk area is πR_sun^2, the observed area ratio is r=5.16×10^-7. Small rounding errors can produce large changes in spherical excess; using a nearly flat triangle also gives full credit and yields r≈5.13×10^-7.
caption: Figure 2: Solar magnetograms taken at the end of January 2020.

question: Figure 2 shows two magnetograms of the Sun taken with the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) at the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) toward the end of January 2020. The picture on the left was taken three days after the image on the right. If an observer on Earth uses a huge f/5 telescope with focal length 13 m to look at this sunspot, will it be possible to resolve it? Visible light is centered at 550 nm.
answer: The telescope diameter is from f/D=5, so 13/D=5 and D=2.6 m. The angular resolution is θ=1.22λ/D=1.22×5.5×10^-7/2.6=2.58×10^-7 rad. The smallest side length is l=2πR_sun×0.0981°/360°=1.19×10^6 m. Correcting for inclination gives l_c=1.19×10^6 cos(52.2°)=7.31×10^5 m. The angular size is α=7.31×10^5/(1.496×10^11)=4.89×10^-6 rad. Since α>θ, it is possible to resolve the sunspot.
caption: Figure 2: Solar magnetograms taken at the end of January 2020.

question: Figure 2 shows two magnetograms of the Sun taken with the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) at the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) toward the end of January 2020. The picture on the left was taken three days after the image on the right. The Sun generates its luminosity by converting hydrogen into helium in the proton-proton chain. In the most energetic branch, 4 protons fuse into a helium nucleus. Considering that only 10% of the solar mass can be converted into energy, calculate the time that the Sun spends in the Main Sequence.
answer: Mass change per reaction: Δm = 4m_H − m_He = 4×1.6725×10^-27 kg − 6.644×10^-27 kg = 4.600×10^-29 kg. Fraction of mass converted is f = Δm/(4m_H)=6.876×10^-3. Mass converted into energy during the Main Sequence is ΔM = M f 0.10 = 1.989×10^30×6.876×10^-3×0.10 = 1.368×10^27 kg. Total energy is E=ΔMc^2 = 1.229×10^44 J. Time is Δt=E/L = 1.229×10^44 J/(3.826×10^26 W)=3.213×10^17 s ≈ 10 billion years.
